slides.text: November 28, 1933. The last morning of Gandhi's second and final visit to Chhattisgarh. He will never return. The land does not know this. He does not know this. Only history knows — and history says nothing until it is already too late.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Dawn over Raipur, November 28, 1933. The city quiet in early morning light. Shukla Niwas where Gandhi stayed. A lamp still burning in his room. The last morning. Its finality invisible, unknowable, irreversible. Warm and melancholic light.

slides.text: Gandhi rose before dawn, as always. His morning routine: prayer, spinning, a brief correspondence with Mahadev Desai. The same routine in every place he stayed. The consistency of a man who lived by practice, not by circumstance.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's morning routine at Shukla Niwas — the charkha spinning in the early light, prayer in the quiet room, Desai writing nearby. The same routine as every other morning. The last morning indistinguishable from the others — which is its own kind of grace.

slides.text: Ravi Shankar Shukla — in whose home Gandhi had stayed — was there for the last morning. The man who had received Gandhi as DCC secretary in 1920, who had housed him in 1933. Thirteen years of a relationship reaching its final Chhattisgarh morning.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla at Shukla Niwas on the last morning — serving tea, speaking quietly with Gandhi. The host and the guest on their last morning together. Shukla's face carrying what he cannot say: please stay, come back, do not go. Gandhi's face: gratitude, also unspeakable.

slides.text: The last morning began with a final gathering at Shukla Niwas — the inner circle of Chhattisgarh's movement leadership. Sharma, Shukla, Srivastava, Meghawale, Gupta, Rao. The people who had made the visit possible and who had given the most to the movement.
slides.visualDescription: The final gathering at Shukla Niwas — the inner circle. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma, Ravi Shankar Shukla, Babu Chhotelal Srivastava, Narayan Rao Meghawale, Ghanshyam Singh Gupta, E. Raghavendra Rao. Gandhi in the center. The movement's leadership in one room for the last time.

slides.text: Gandhi spoke to each person individually before the general farewell. With Pt. Sharma: the conversation about the Satnam Ashram, about untouchability, about the thirteen years of work that made Gandhi call him guru. A private conversation in a quiet corner.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi and Pt. Sundarlal Sharma in a quiet corner of Shukla Niwas — the private farewell conversation. Gandhi holding Sharma's hands. The guru and his student in one last exchange. The things said between them: known only to them. The privacy of the deepest honours.

slides.text: With Srivastava: Gandhi asking what he planned to do next for the Harijan cause. Srivastava answering: the same thing I have always done — be present, organise, refuse to accept injustice. Gandhi: that is all I ask of anyone. That is enough.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's private farewell with Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — asking about plans for the Harijan cause. Srivastava's answer. Gandhi's response: that is enough. Two men who share the 1920 Kandel memory in their deepest identity, saying goodbye for what neither knows is the last time.

slides.text: With Shukla: the acknowledgement of what the DCC had built since 1920 — thirteen years of an organisation that had survived Non-Cooperation withdrawal, arrests, the Swaraj years, the Salt March era. Gandhi to Shukla: you built something that outlasts any single man's presence.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's farewell to Ravi Shankar Shukla — acknowledging what Shukla had built since signing the DCC papers in 1920. The organisation that had outlasted everything. Gandhi naming this as Shukla's greatest achievement. Shukla receiving it. The first secretary of the first DCC being honoured by the man who inspired its founding.

slides.text: A last morning prayer session — the group gathered together for Gandhi's morning prayer. The charkha beside him. The room quiet. The prayer as a form of community — gathering what cannot be said into something that does not need words. Silence shared.
slides.visualDescription: The morning prayer at Shukla Niwas — Gandhi leading, the inner circle gathered. The charkha beside him. Complete silence except for Gandhi's prayer. The room carrying the weight of five days, thirteen years, and the goodbye that is approaching. Silence as the fullest expression.

slides.text: After the prayer, the final accounting of the visit: funds collected for the Harijan Sevak Sangh across all the meetings. Contributions from Durg, Raipur, Bilaspur, Dhamtari, the village circuit. The total becoming the practical foundation for future Harijan work.
slides.visualDescription: Mahadev Desai totaling the Harijan Sevak Sangh collections — city by city, village by village. The total representing five days across Chhattisgarh. The practical resource that the visit built. The Harijan cause now funded by this province's generosity. Numbers as commitment.

slides.text: The Harijan Sevak Sangh work that Gandhi organised in Chhattisgarh during the second visit would continue for years after his departure. The schools, the temple entry work, the community organising — seeded in five days, sustained by the people who remained.
slides.visualDescription: The Harijan Sevak Sangh work after Gandhi's departure — schools opening, temples continuing to accept Harijan entry, community organising continuing. The five days seeding years of work. Gandhi departing; his mission remaining. The structure outlasting the visit.

slides.text: November 28, 1933. Raipur station. The same station that received Gandhi on December 20, 1920. The same platform that had seen the third-class compartment arrival that moved 15,000 people. Now the departure platform. The same space, different emotional weight.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur station, November 28, 1933 — the same platform as December 20, 1920. The crowd gathered but different in mood: the 1920 arrival was joy and anticipation. The 1933 departure is gratitude and grief. The same stone under different feet feeling different things.

slides.text: The crowd at the departure platform was large — word had spread that Gandhi was leaving. People came to see him one more time. Some had been at the 1920 arrival. Some had been at the Victoria Garden meeting. Some had never seen him and feared they never would again.
slides.visualDescription: The departure platform crowd — diverse in its relationship to the visit. The 1920 veterans. The Victoria Garden thousand. Those who missed all the meetings and came now out of a need they cannot name. The crowd of farewell as different from the crowd of welcome.

slides.text: Mahadev Desai carried the bags. Meera Ben carried what she always carried: her quiet presence, her Indian dress, her English accent that was the most disarming argument against the idea that India's freedom was only for Indians. A disciple defined by her journey to Gandhi.
slides.visualDescription: Meera Ben at the departure platform — carrying her bag, in her Indian sari, looking at the Chhattisgarh landscape for the last time with Gandhi. Her presence: the most complete rebuttal to colonial racism. An Englishwoman who chose India so completely she became it.

slides.text: Thakkar Bapa at the platform — the welfare worker who had made the detailed village assessment. His notebook filled with what Chhattisgarh's tribal and Harijan communities needed from the Harijan Sevak Sangh. He was not saying goodbye to a place. He was carrying a task.
slides.visualDescription: Thakkar Bapa at the departure platform, his assessment notebook in hand. Not primarily saying goodbye to a place — carrying forward the task. His mind already on what he will do with the information gathered in the village circuit. Purpose as the departure gift.

slides.text: Gandhi walked toward the train. People touched his feet. He folded his hands in namaste to those he could not reach. The same hands that had accepted Makhan's haircut, that had held Sharma's hands, that had spread open for the Tilak Fund in 1920. These hands, leaving.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi walking toward the train — people touching his feet as he passes, he folding his hands to those he cannot reach. His hands visible in close-up — the same hands that had done so much in five days. The hands leaving. The platform receiving his last steps on Chhattisgarh ground.

slides.text: He boarded the train. Third class. Of course. The same choice as 1920. The choice that had made 15,000 people see who he really was when he arrived. Now the same choice on departure — consistency as the deepest form of character.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi boarding the third-class compartment at Raipur station — the same choice as 1920. The crowd watching. Some of them remember the 1920 moment. The same compartment type. The same man. Thirteen years and the choice unchanged. Character as consistency across time.

slides.text: The train began to move. Gandhi at the window — the same position as arrival in 1920, hands folded in namaste, Chhattisgarh scrolling past. The platform crowd not moving. People standing still as the train moved away. Watching until nothing remained to watch.
slides.visualDescription: The train moving from Raipur station — Gandhi at the window, hands folded. The platform crowd standing still, watching. The train pulling away slowly. The gap between the platform and the last carriage growing. People not moving. The departure as a ceremony of stillness.

slides.text: The platform after the train left. People standing where they stood, not yet ready to leave. The space still carrying the shape of what had been there — the crowds of the two visits, the DCC founding, the Tilak Fund, the 15,000 at Gandhi Chowk. All of it present in absence.
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur platform after the train's departure — people slowly, reluctantly dispersing. The platform emptying. The space still carrying the imprint of what had been there. The absence of Gandhi as its own kind of presence. History settling into the stones of the platform.

slides.text: In the train: Gandhi looked out the window at Chhattisgarh. The Sal forest. The paddy fields. The small stations — each one a name that carries a story. He did not know he was looking at this for the last time. The last sight without the weight of last-ness.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the train window — the Chhattisgarh landscape scrolling past. Forest. Fields. Small stations with their name boards. His eyes taking in what he does not know he is seeing for the last time. The mercy of not knowing last-ness. The landscape received as itself.

slides.text: Mahadev Desai wrote in his diary on November 28, 1933: 'The five days in Chhattisgarh have been among the most significant of the entire Harijan tour. The people here have done remarkable things in the decade since Gandhi's first visit.'
slides.visualDescription: Mahadev Desai's November 28 diary entry — his handwriting, the words visible. His assessment: five significant days. The people's remarkable decade. The historian-in-residence recording what he witnessed. The diary as the most authoritative document of the second visit.

slides.text: The five days were over. Gandhi had spoken to one lakh at Victoria Garden. Had eaten with Harijan children at the Baithd School. Had named Tamora as Gandhigram. Had called Sharma his guru. Had made a promise to Bilaspur he would not keep. Had opened doors.
slides.visualDescription: The five days summarised in sequence — Victoria Garden, Baithd School meal, Gandhigram naming, Sharma as guru, Bilaspur promise, Kurud temple door. Each image appearing in turn. The five days as a complete work. The summary as its own kind of farewell.

slides.text: Gandhi left Chhattisgarh on November 28, 1933. He would not return. He would be assassinated fifteen years later, on January 30, 1948, in New Delhi. His last decade was the most turbulent of his life — partition, independence, the violence he spent his life fighting.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi departing Chhattisgarh — then the fifteen years compressed: 1935 withdrawal from Congress, 1942 Quit India, 1945 independence negotiations, 1947 partition, 1948 assassination. The last decade of a man who never stopped. His Chhattisgarh farewell as his last peace.

slides.text: The people Gandhi left behind in Chhattisgarh: Pt. Sharma, who would continue his Harijan work until his death. Shukla, who would become the first Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh in 1947. Srivastava, who would continue in Dhamtari until the very end.
slides.visualDescription: The people Gandhi left behind — Sharma, Shukla, Srivastava — continuing. Sharma until his death. Shukla to 1947 as CM. Srivastava to the very end. Their continuity as the completion of what Gandhi started. The work outlasting the visitor. The mission outlasting the missionary.

slides.text: August 15, 1947. India becomes independent. Ravi Shankar Shukla hoists the flag at Sitabardi Fort, Nagpur — the first Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh. Twenty-seven years after signing the DCC papers in Gandhi's presence, the thread complete. One man's full arc.
slides.visualDescription: August 15, 1947 — Ravi Shankar Shukla at Sitabardi Fort, Nagpur, hoisting the Indian tricolor as first CM of Madhya Pradesh. The same hands that signed the DCC papers in 1920. The arc from Gandhi's first visit to independence, complete in one man's life.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma died in 1940 — seven years after Gandhi called him guru, seven years before independence. He did not live to see free India. But free India would not have been possible without what he had built. The man who prepared the ground, not harvesting the crop.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma's death in 1940 — seven years before independence. His grave. The nation he prepared for but did not live to see. The farmer who tills and plants and does not live to harvest. His legacy: the Satnam Ashram, the Janeu movement, Gandhi's guru-acknowledgement.

slides.text: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — the organiser of the Kandel Satyagraha — continued his work in Dhamtari through independence and beyond. His Satyagraha: the most local of victories. His commitment: the most universal of qualities. He is the heart of this story.
slides.visualDescription: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava continuing through independence — in Dhamtari, working. The canal still flowing. His Satyagraha still the city's defining moment. The man who started everything in a flooded paddy field in August 1920, still present, still committed, in a free India.

slides.text: The last morning in Chhattisgarh — November 28, 1933 — was also the last morning of a specific era. The era of Gandhi's physical presence. After this, Chhattisgarh would carry his ideas, his method, his inspiration — but not his body. The ideas proved stronger.
slides.visualDescription: November 28, 1933 — the last morning of Gandhi's physical presence in Chhattisgarh. Then: the decades after. The ideas continuing. The method practised. The Satyagrahas remembered. The organisations functioning. The ideas proved stronger than the body that carried them.

slides.text: The last morning: Gandhi at the window of the departing train. The land of 36 forts receiving his departure. The Sal forest. The rivers. The paddy fields. The small stations. This land held his two visits like a book holds its chapters — firmly, completely, permanently.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's last sight of Chhattisgarh from the train window — the land receiving his departure. The Sal forest. The rivers. The paddy fields. The 36 forts in the distance. The land as a book holding its two chapters. The train taking him away. The land staying.

slides.text: The train crossed the Chhattisgarh border. Gandhi's last morning in this land was over. The book of his two visits was closed. But the chapters do not close — they continue in everyone who read them. In every Satyagrahi who acted in his absence. In every temple that opened its door.
slides.visualDescription: The train crossing the Chhattisgarh border — the land ending behind it. Gandhi in the compartment. The book of the two visits closed. But in Chhattisgarh behind the border: the chapters continuing. The Satyagrahis still acting. The doors still opening. The book read forever.

slides.text: 'Gandhi came to Chhattisgarh twice — the first time as Mohandas, the second time as a Mahatma. During both these visits Gandhi influenced the society and every person of Chhattisgarh.' — Johar Gandhi, by Amir Hashmi.
slides.visualDescription: The book's words on screen — the source text acknowledged. Two visits. Two names. Two missions. One land. One love. The book Johar Gandhi as the archive of what history forgot to keep. The words carrying the weight of years of research and recovered memory.

slides.text: Three more episodes remain in this series. The story is not over. The people Gandhi left behind continued for fourteen more years. Their stories — the Gandhi Chowk, the women of the movement, the promise of Johar — deserve their full telling.
slides.visualDescription: The series continuing beyond the departure — Episodes 8, 9, 10 still ahead. The stories of those left behind, the meaning of Gandhi Chowk, the women of the movement, the final Johar. The last morning is not the end. The story continues in those who stayed.

slides.text: November 28, 1933. The train moves north and west toward Wardha and Sevagram. Gandhi is working already — letters to dictate, plans to make, the next stops of the Harijan tour to organise. The last morning already becoming the next day's beginning.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi on the train working — Desai writing at his dictation. Letters being composed. The next stops of the Harijan tour being discussed. The last morning of Chhattisgarh already behind him; the next challenge already ahead. A man who does not pause between purposes.

slides.text: What Gandhi took from Chhattisgarh: the intelligence of what ordinary people can do without a leader present. The Kandel Satyagraha. The Tamora seventeen days. The Baithd School since 1926. The salt-making in Dhamtari. Chhattisgarh as proof of the method's independence.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi on the train processing what he learned from Chhattisgarh — the method's independence proved. Kandel won before he arrived. Tamora's seventeen days without him. Baithd School since 1926 without his visit. The ideas had taken root and grown without the gardener.

slides.text: What Chhattisgarh took from Gandhi: two visits. Thirty-five years of inspiration drawn from three days in 1920 and five days in 1933. Eight days in a land of 36 forts that used those eight days to fuel a century of commitment.
slides.visualDescription: Eight days total — three in 1920, five in 1933. Against 35 years of the freedom movement in Chhattisgarh that those eight days touched and shaped. The mathematics of inspiration: eight days multiplied by decades of commitment equals the story of Chhattisgarh's freedom.

slides.text: The last morning: complete. Gandhi has left. Chhattisgarh remains. The work continues. The canal still flows. The temple doors — some of them — stay open. The DCC still meets. The charkha still turns. The Satyagraha method still works. The land still holds.
slides.visualDescription: Chhattisgarh after Gandhi's departure — the land continuing its daily life. The Kandel canal. The Raipur DCC. The charkha spinning in someone's home. The open temple. The national school. Everything he touched continuing. The morning after the last morning.

slides.text: Three episodes remain: the Gandhi Chowk that carries his name, the women of the movement who are half the story, and the final Johar — the greeting and farewell that this land gives to the man and the memory. The series approaching its completion.
slides.visualDescription: A preview of the final three episodes: Gandhi Chowk as living memorial, the women of the movement as the story's other half, the final Johar as the series' ending. The approach to the ending as its own kind of beginning. The completion that is also a continuation.

slides.text: The last morning was also the first morning of everything that followed. Next: Episode 8 — Gandhi Chowk.
slides.visualDescription: The departing train becoming smaller on the horizon. Then: present-day Gandhi Chowk, Raipur — the intersection that carries his name. The past and present in one image. The last morning becoming the first morning of a living legacy. Title: Episode 8 — Gandhi Chowk.
